title: The Sumerian City-States
subtitle: 2900–2334 BC · Rival Cities on the King List, the Lagash–Umma War, the Tombs of Ur, and the First Unification

categories.label: Power
categories.subtitle: Kingship rotating between the cities of the Sumerian King List, the hegemony of Kish, the dynasty of Lagash and its border war with Umma, the tombs of the kings of Ur, and Lugalzagesi's brief unification

entries.group: The King List and the First Dynasty of Kish
entries.label: Etana and the kings before history
entries.hint: The Sumerian King List opens after the Flood with kingship 'lowered from heaven' to Kish, and a line of rulers with fantastic reign-lengths — among them Etana, 'the shepherd who ascended to heaven and made firm all the lands', a hero of later legend. None can be verified, but the list encodes a claim: that Kish held the first legitimate kingship over the land.
entries.note: Thorkild Jacobsen, 'The Sumerian King List' (AS 11, 1939); the Etana legend edited by J. V. Kinnier Wilson (1985).

entries.label: En-mebaragesi and Aga — the record begins
entries.hint: En-mebaragesi of Kish is the earliest Sumerian ruler attested by his own inscriptions — two stone fragments naming him — and the King List credits him with carrying off the weapons of Elam. His son Aga besieged Uruk and features in the Sumerian poem 'Gilgamesh and Aga', in which the men of Uruk refuse to submit. With them, Sumerian history leaves legend for documented fact.
entries.note: En-mebaragesi vase inscriptions in Douglas Frayne, RIME 1 (2008); 'Gilgamesh and Aga' edited by Dina Katz (1993).

entries.label: 'King of Kish' — the title of overlordship
entries.hint: Whichever Sumerian ruler claimed leadership over the whole land took the title lugal Kiš, 'king of Kish' — worn by rulers of Ur, Lagash, Uruk and Umma who never governed Kish itself, and later by Sargon of Akkad. Kish, commanding the narrow neck where the Tigris and Euphrates run closest, had become the symbol of hegemony over Sumer as a whole.
entries.note: William Hallo, 'Early Mesopotamian Royal Titles' (1957); the title's use tracked across the Presargonic inscriptions (Cooper 1986).

entries.label: Mesalim, the overlord who drew the line
entries.hint: King Mesalim of Kish was acknowledged across southern Sumer: he dedicated a mace-head at Lagash and a bowl at Adab, and — most consequentially — he surveyed and set a boundary stele between Lagash and Umma along the divine command of Ishtaran. That line, and its repeated violation, drives the next century and a half of southern politics.
entries.note: Mesalim's dedications in Frayne, RIME 1; his boundary settlement reconstructed in Jerrold Cooper, 'Reconstructing History: The Lagash–Umma Border Conflict' (1983).

entries.label: Gilgamesh of Uruk
entries.hint: The King List makes Bilgames — Gilgamesh — the fifth king of Uruk's first dynasty, and a later tradition credits him with building the city wall and the Ninlil temple at Nippur. No contemporary inscription of his survives, but a ruler of that name and rough date is plausible, and by the Ur III period he was a god, a judge of the dead, and the hero of a poem cycle that became the world's first epic.
entries.note: The King List (Jacobsen 1939); the Sumerian Gilgamesh poems and the epic in Andrew George, 'The Babylonian Gilgamesh Epic' (2003).

entries.label: Mesannepada and the First Dynasty of Ur
entries.hint: Mesannepada, 'king of Ur, king of Kish', is the first ruler of Ur fixed by contemporary evidence — his name inscribed on a lapis bead found at Mari, five hundred kilometres away, a measure of the reach of his contacts. His predecessors Meskalamdug and Akalamdug are known chiefly from the gold and the graves of Ur's Royal Cemetery, which belongs to this dynasty's world.
entries.note: Mesannepada bead and inscriptions in Frayne, RIME 1; the dynasty and the cemetery in Leonard Woolley, 'Ur Excavations II: The Royal Cemetery' (1934).

entries.label: Puabi of Ur
entries.loc: Found: Ur (grave PG 800) · Now: British Museum & Penn Museum
entries.hint: In one of the great tombs of the Royal Cemetery lay a woman about forty, adorned with a headdress of gold leaves and lapis, her name and the title nin — 'lady' or 'queen' — cut on three cylinder seals beside her. Buried with her were dozens of attendants, wagons and oxen. Whether Puabi ruled in her own right, was a king's consort, or was a high priestess of the moon-god is unresolved; that she held real standing is not.
entries.note: Woolley, 'Ur Excavations II' (1934); re-analysis in Richard Zettler & Lee Horne (eds.), 'Treasures from the Royal Tombs of Ur' (1998).

entries.label: Ur-Nanshe founds the house of Lagash
entries.hint: Ur-Nanshe of Lagash built temples, dug canals, imported timber by ship from Dilmun, and left a series of dedication reliefs — one showing him carrying a builder's basket of clay on his head, his wife and named sons around him. His reign begins the richest documentary record of the Early Dynastic age: the archives of Lagash, from which most of what we know of ED society is drawn.
entries.note: Ur-Nanshe inscriptions and reliefs in Frayne, RIME 1, and Jerrold Cooper, 'Presargonic Inscriptions' (1986).

entries.label: Eannatum, 'who subjugated all the lands'
entries.hint: Eannatum, Ur-Nanshe's grandson, made Lagash briefly the strongest power in Sumer: he crushed Umma and reimposed the border, and campaigned against Ur, Uruk, Kish, Elam, Mari and the Iranian highlands, taking the title 'king of Kish'. His victory over Umma is carved on the Stele of the Vultures, the first war monument. His empire did not outlast him.
entries.note: Eannatum's inscriptions (the 'Stele of the Vultures' text, the Mesilim cone) in Cooper, 'Presargonic Inscriptions' (1986); Frayne, RIME 1.

entries.label: Enannatum I and Entemena
entries.hint: Eannatum's brother Enannatum I and nephew Entemena held Lagash at its most prosperous. Entemena's inscribed clay cone lays out the whole Umma dispute from Mesalim onward as a legal brief, and he made a treaty of 'brotherhood' with Lugal-kinishe-dudu of Uruk — the earliest known interstate parity treaty. His silver libation vase, worked with the lion-headed eagle of Ningirsu, is a masterpiece of ED metalwork.
entries.note: Entemena cone and vase in Cooper, 'Presargonic Inscriptions' (1986) and 'Reconstructing History' (1983); the vase in the Louvre.

entries.label: Urukagina and the reform edict
entries.hint: Urukagina (his name may read Uru-inim-gina), coming to power in Lagash outside the ruling line, issued a text describing abuses he had ended — officials seizing the property of the poor, priests overcharging for burials, the palace encroaching on temple and citizen land — and claimed to have made a covenant with the god Ningirsu 'that the powerful man would not oppress the orphan and the widow'. It is the first recorded programme of social reform.
entries.note: The reform texts (Ukg. 1, 4–6, 15) in Cooper, 'Presargonic Inscriptions' (1986); analysis in Samuel Noah Kramer, 'The Sumerians' (1963) and Piotr Steinkeller.

entries.label: Lugalzagesi unites the land
entries.hint: Lugalzagesi, governor of Umma, broke Lagash and burned its temples, then took Uruk and made it his capital, claiming from Enlil at Nippur kingship over all Sumer 'from the Lower Sea, along the Tigris and Euphrates, to the Upper Sea'. It was the first time one man ruled the whole of Sumer. Twenty-odd years later Sargon of Akkad defeated him and led him in a neck-stock to the gate of Enlil.
entries.note: Lugalzagesi's Nippur vase inscription in Frayne, RIME 1; his fall recorded in Sargon's inscriptions (Frayne, RIME 2).

entries.label: The Sumerian King List and rotating kingship
entries.hint: The King List presents Sumerian history as a single kingship passing from one city to the next — Kish, then Uruk, then Ur, then elsewhere — never held by two cities at once, moving by the will of the gods. Real Early Dynastic Sumer was a scatter of rival states holding power simultaneously. The List is not a chronicle but a charter: an argument that legitimate rule over the land is one and indivisible, and belongs to whoever currently holds it.
entries.note: Jacobsen, 'The Sumerian King List' (1939); the ideological reading in Piotr Michalowski, 'History as Charter' (JAOS 1983).

categories.label: Conflict
categories.subtitle: The first documented war — Lagash against Umma over the Gu'edena — the phalanx of the Stele of the Vultures, the battle-wagons of the Standard of Ur, and the sack of Lagash

entries.label: Lagash against Umma — the first recorded war
entries.loc: the Gu'edena, between Girsu and Umma
entries.hint: For some five generations Lagash and Umma fought over the Gu'edena, a strip of fertile canal-fed land on their border. King Mesalim of Kish had set a boundary stele there; Umma repeatedly ploughed across it and diverted its water, Lagash repeatedly drove them back. It is the earliest war anywhere for which both the cause and the course are written down — by the Lagash side, at length and with grievance.
entries.note: Reconstructed from the Lagash inscriptions in Jerrold Cooper, 'Reconstructing History: The Lagash–Umma Border Conflict' (1983).

entries.label: The Stele of the Vultures
entries.loc: Found: Girsu (Telloh) · Now: Musée du Louvre
entries.hint: Eannatum's limestone victory stele carries the war on two registers. On the divine side the god Ningirsu holds a net full of struggling enemies and brains them with a mace. On the human side Eannatum leads a tight block of helmeted, shielded spearmen marching over a heap of the enemy dead while vultures fly off with severed heads. It is the earliest image of a disciplined infantry formation — the phalanx — and of a state at organised war.
entries.note: Louvre; the definitive study is Irene Winter, 'After the Battle is Over: The Stele of the Vultures and the Beginning of Historical Narrative in the Art of the Ancient Near East' (1985).

entries.label: The war-wagons of the Standard of Ur
entries.loc: Found: Ur (Royal Cemetery) · Now: British Museum
entries.hint: An inlaid wooden box from a royal grave at Ur shows the Early Dynastic army: four-wheeled battle-wagons drawn by onagers rolling over fallen enemies, files of spearmen in studded cloaks, axemen, and naked bound prisoners driven before the king. The other face shows the victory feast. Together they picture the two things a Sumerian ruler was for — to win the war and to preside over the plenty that followed.
entries.note: British Museum (BM 121201); Woolley, 'Ur Excavations II' (1934); military reading in Robert Rollinger and in the essays in Zettler & Horne (1998).

entries.label: The contest for the leadership of the land
entries.loc: Kish, Uruk, Ur, Lagash and Umma
entries.hint: Behind the Gu'edena quarrel ran a larger, shifting struggle for primacy — Kish against Uruk in 'Gilgamesh and Aga', Ur's kings claiming Kish, Eannatum of Lagash storming across the whole south and into Elam, Enshakushana of Uruk sacking Kish and taking its king prisoner. No city held the lead for long, and the title everyone wanted, 'king of Kish', was worth having precisely because it was contested.
entries.note: The hegemony sequence in the Presargonic inscriptions (Cooper 1986; Frayne, RIME 1); overview in Marc Van De Mieroop, 'A History of the Ancient Near East' (2016).

entries.label: The sack of Lagash and the lament for it
entries.hint: When Lugalzagesi of Umma overran Lagash he burned the shrines of Girsu, Antasura, Nina and the rest, and carried off their silver and precious stones. A scribe of the defeated Urukagina wrote a short text cataloguing each act of desecration and ending: 'The man of Umma, having sacked Lagash, has committed a sin against Ningirsu... May his goddess Nisaba make him bear the sin.' It is the earliest formal indictment of an enemy for sacrilege in war.
entries.note: The 'Lament for Lagash' (Ukg. 16) in Cooper, 'Presargonic Inscriptions' (1986); discussed in Piotr Michalowski, 'The Lamentation over the Destruction of Sumer and Ur' (1989), intro.

entries.label: The walled city and the guarded gate
entries.hint: Every Early Dynastic city of consequence was walled — Uruk's great circuit was already ancient — and the temple itself might be a fortress, as at Khafajah, where the oval sanctuary sat inside its own double enclosure. The city gate was where courts sat, deals were struck and treaties sworn, a defended threshold that was also the city's public room.
entries.note: Khafajah Temple Oval in Pinhas Delougaz, 'The Temple Oval at Khafajah' (OIP 53, 1940); ED fortification surveyed in Roger Matthews, 'The Archaeology of Mesopotamia' (2003).

categories.label: Order
categories.subtitle: The é and the ensí, the temple estate and the rise of the palace, standard weights and the city-seal, and the reform edict of Urukagina

entries.label: The ensí, the lugal and the god's estate
entries.hint: A Sumerian ruler was in principle the manager of his city-god's household. The commonest title, ensí, means roughly 'governor' or 'steward'; lugal, 'big man', claimed more — kingship, often over other cities too. The ruler held the land as the god's tenant and answered to the god for it. Beside the temple, a distinct royal residence, the é-gal or 'big house', was now taking shape as an institution in its own right.
entries.note: Thorkild Jacobsen, 'Early Political Development in Mesopotamia' (ZA 1957); Piotr Steinkeller, 'On Rulers, Priests and Sacred Marriage' (1999).

entries.label: The palace encroaches on the temple estate
entries.hint: The Lagash archives show the city-god's estate — the households of Ningirsu and the goddess Bau — as the dominant landholder and employer. But under the last kings the royal household and the queen's household were absorbing temple land, appointing their own men to priesthoods, and taxing what had been the god's. Urukagina's reform text is one side's account of that quarrel between crown and cult.
entries.note: Gebhard Selz, 'Untersuchungen zur Götterwelt des altsumerischen Stadtstaates von Lagaš' (1995); the estate figures in Benjamin Foster, 'A New Look at the Sumerian Temple State' (1981).

entries.label: The é-mí — the queen's household
entries.hint: The 'house of the woman', é-mí, was the estate of the ruler's wife — under Baranamtara, wife of Lugalanda, and Shasha, wife of Urukagina, a great agricultural and textile enterprise with well over a thousand dependent workers and its own detailed archive. Sumerian queens conducted diplomacy by gift-exchange with other courts and endowed temples in their own name. It is the clearest early evidence for institutional economic power in women's hands.
entries.note: Kazuya Maekawa, 'The Development of the é-mí in Lagash' (1973); the Baranamtara and Shasha archives, published across the Presargonic Lagash text corpus.

entries.label: Weight, measure and the sealed standard
entries.hint: Trade and taxation ran on shared units — the shekel, mina and talent for weight; the sila and gur for grain; the sar for area — checked against official stone weights and sealed measuring vessels. Rulers advertised 'just' weights as a mark of good government, and Urukagina's reforms include a promise to stop officials cheating with false measures.
entries.note: Marvin Powell, 'Masse und Gewichte' (Reallexikon der Assyriologie VII, 1990); the ideology of just measures in the reform texts (Cooper 1986).

entries.label: Law without a code
entries.loc: Found: southern Sumer · Now: British Museum & dispersed
entries.hint: No Early Dynastic law code survives, and there may have been none — but the legal order is visible everywhere else: engraved stone tablets recording sales of land before named witnesses (the 'Blau monuments' and their kin), the settlement of lawsuits, oaths sworn by the king and the city-god, and rulers' claims to have protected the weak against the strong. Written law codes come two centuries later, at Ur.
entries.note: Claus Wilcke, 'Early Ancient Near Eastern Law' (2007); the archaic land-sale documents (kudurrus) catalogued by Ignace Gelb, Piotr Steinkeller & Robert Whiting, 'Earliest Land Tenure Systems in the Near East' (1991).

entries.label: Nippur, the Tummal and the league of cities
entries.hint: The southern cities — 'Sumer', ki-en-gi — seem to have shared cultic duties toward Enlil at Nippur, taking turns to maintain his sanctuary and the shrine of the Tummal, whose upkeep the later 'Tummal Inscription' records ruler by ruler. Nippur held no army and conquered nobody; it was the neutral ground where a claim to lead the land was ratified. Whether this amounted to a formal 'Kengir League' is debated.
entries.note: Thorkild Jacobsen, 'The Tummal Inscription' (JCS 1953); the league idea and its critics in Piotr Michalowski, 'Mental Maps and Ideology' (1993).

categories.label: Belief
categories.subtitle: Nippur and Enlil as the fount of legitimacy, the city-god theology, the votive statue of the eternal worshipper, and the death pits of Ur

entries.label: Enlil of Nippur, giver of kingship
entries.hint: Enlil, whose house the E-kur stood at Nippur, was the executive of the divine assembly — the god who set destinies and, above all, who granted or withdrew the kingship of the land. Rulers from every rival city sought his sanction and rebuilt his temple. Nippur itself stayed out of politics, and that is exactly why its blessing was worth having: it belonged to no faction.
entries.note: Nippur excavations published in the OIP series (McCown, Haines, Gibson); Enlil's role in W. G. Lambert, 'Babylonian Creation Myths' (2013) and Jacobsen, 'The Treasures of Darkness' (1976).

entries.label: The city and its god
entries.hint: Each Sumerian city belonged to a deity — Nanna the moon at Ur, Inanna at Uruk, Enki at Eridu, Ningirsu at Lagash, Shara at Umma — who lived in its main temple, owned much of its land, and was fed, clothed and entertained by the citizens as a great householder. To be a citizen was to be part of the god's estate; a war between cities was, in the telling, a quarrel between their gods.
entries.note: Gebhard Selz on the Lagash pantheon (1995); the 'divine household' model in Jacobsen, 'The Treasures of Darkness' (1976).

entries.label: The pantheon and the god-lists
entries.hint: The tablets from Fara and Abu Salabikh include the earliest god-lists — hundreds of divine names set in a fixed order that ranks the pantheon, headed by An the sky, Enlil, Enki and the mother-goddess. To list the gods in order was itself a theological act: it fixed who outranked whom in the assembly that governed the universe, and the ordering barely changed for two thousand years.
entries.note: The Fara god-list edited by Manfred Krebernik; the Abu Salabikh texts in Robert Biggs, 'Inscriptions from Tell Abu Salabikh' (OIP 99, 1974).

entries.label: The votive statue — the eternal worshipper
entries.loc: Found: Tell Asmar (Square Temple) · Now: Iraq Museum & Oriental Institute
entries.hint: An Early Dynastic worshipper could commission a small stone image of himself — standing, hands clasped at the chest, enormous eyes inlaid with shell and dark stone, sometimes inscribed 'it offers prayers' — and set it in the god's temple to stand before the deity forever on his behalf. A cache of a dozen, buried under the floor of the Square Temple at Tell Asmar, is the type-find.
entries.note: Henri Frankfort, 'Sculpture of the Third Millennium B.C. from Tell Asmar and Khafajah' (OIP 44, 1939); Jean Evans, 'The Lives of Sumerian Sculpture' (2012).

entries.label: The death pits of Ur
entries.hint: In the largest tombs of Ur, the ruler was buried with a household that went into the grave too — soldiers at the door, grooms with the wagon-oxen, women in gold headdresses, musicians with their lyres, dozens of people laid out in rows. Woolley thought they took poison willingly; forensic re-study of the skulls found blunt-force wounds, and traces of heating and mercury that suggest the bodies were treated and displayed. Nothing like it recurs in Mesopotamia.
entries.note: Woolley, 'Ur Excavations II' (1934); the forensic re-analysis in Aubrey Baadsgaard, Janet Monge & Richard Zettler, 'Bludgeoned, Burned, and Beautified' (2011) and their Antiquity paper.

entries.label: The festival year
entries.hint: The temple set the calendar: monthly offerings, the great seasonal festivals, the barley-eating and malt-eating feasts of Ningirsu at Lagash, the Tummal festival at Nippur, and at the turn of the year a rite in which the ruler, as the god's steward, was joined to the goddess to renew the land's fertility. Religion here was less a set of beliefs than a year-round schedule of feeding and honouring the divine landlords.
entries.note: The Lagash festival calendar in Gebhard Selz (1995); the year-rite ('sacred marriage') debated in Steinkeller, 'On Rulers, Priests and Sacred Marriage' (1999).
